definition: Exculpate means to free someone from guilt or blame.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word exculpate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know exculpate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Three independent witnesses placed the peddler two counties away, and their sworn statements exculpated him before the assizes even convened.
A lawyer defends a client whether or not the proof favors her; defend stops far short of exculpate, which means the blame is actually lifted.
To clear a name is the everyday phrase for the same rescue; clear stops just short of exculpate, the formal word for blame removed by proof.

Absolve is the ceremonial member of the clearing family: a priest, a panel, or a court declares the burden lifted, and it can cover duties and debts as well as guilt. Exculpate is narrower and colder — it is proof that exculpates, evidence pulling a suspect out from under blame.

Acquit is the jury's formal not-guilty at the end of a trial — a verdict that the charge was not proven, delivered in a courtroom. Exculpate needs no courtroom at all: an alibi or a dated receipt can exculpate a suspect before charges are ever drawn up.

Suspicion for the poisoned well fell on the town's unpopular herbalist until the new physician traced the sickness to a cracked cistern; his report exculpated her so thoroughly that the council paid to reglaze the shop windows her neighbors had broken.
Exculpate is built on culpa, 'blame': to exculpate is to pull someone out from under blame, usually by evidence.
It is narrower than absolve — a panel can absolve you of a duty, but it is proof that exculpates you of a suspected wrong.
Exculpate is the evidence-room member of this unit's clearing family: documents, alibis, and records exculpate.
Boards exonerate, authorities absolve, and events vindicate — reach for exculpate when the proof itself does the lifting.

exculpate: To clear a name is the everyday phrase for the same rescue; clear stops just short of exculpate, the formal word for blame removed by proof.
In 1962 the restorer Ana Reyes was quietly dismissed when a hairline crack was found running through the varnish of the portrait she had just cleaned.
The museum's trustees never held a hearing; the timing seemed proof enough.
Fifty years later, conservators photographing the portrait under raking light noticed the crack in an archival image dated a decade before Reyes ever touched the canvas.
The finding exculpated her completely: the damage she was blamed for had been there all along.
The museum amended its records and named its new conservation studio for her, a gesture her grandchildren attended -- proof, one wrote, that evidence outlives embarrassment.
